            if "index_clause" in case["negotiable"]:
                opts = [o for o in case["term_options"]["index_clause"] if o]

        from arena_kit import total_cost
        n.c_alt = total_cost(case, n.alt["terms"]) if n.alt.get("terms", {}).get("unit_price") else float("inf")
        n.relationship = b.get("category_goal") in ("stabilise", "secure_supply")
        n.c_open = min(n.C(t, t.sheets[0]["terms"]) for t in threads.values())
        n._estimate()
        goal = n.goal(0)
        out = []
        for s, t in threads.items():
            sheets = n.meso(t, goal)
            facts = n.facts_for(t)
            ok = all(must_haves_ok(case, sh, t.std) for sh in sheets)
            msg = n.write(t, 0, sheets, None)
            out.append(f"{s[4:]}: {len(sheets)} pkgs {[sh['unit_price'] for sh in sheets]} must-haves {'ok' if ok else 'BROKEN'}, {len(facts)} facts, {len(msg['body'].split())} words")
            bad += not sheets or not ok
        print(f"{cid[5:]:<4} {case['type']:<15} {b.get('category_goal'):<14} target {n.target_c:,.0f} | " + " | ".join(out))

        print(f"{cid[5:]:<4} CRASH", traceback.format_exc().splitlines()[-1])

input.content:
# makeAnother.md · a buyer agent for the Tacto Negotiation Arena

EHL Grand Finale 2026, Tacto track. Our agent negotiates by e-mail with Tacto's supplier bots for Hollerau
Pumpenwerke: price increases, renewals, RFQs with several bidders, bundles, raw-material surcharges, capacity
cuts and quality cases. It closes the deal with the lowest total cost C, or walks away when the alternative is
cheaper. Forked from [tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit](https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit).

Practice board on the evening before the final: mean best score **0.736** over the 10 hosted suppliers, #3 of 24;
a full fresh pass of the final build scores **0.72-0.73** with 10 deals out of 10 and no failed accept.

## How it negotiates

The code decides every number; a language model only writes the words around them.

1. **A target cost.** For every allowed combination of the case's levers (payment days, contract months, lead
   time, Incoterm, index clause, quality terms) the engine solves the unit price at which the supplier's cash
   value equals its estimated cost floor - from our should-cost, its own cost breakdown or letter, its cited
   cost drivers - and costs that package with the arena's published formula. The cheapest one is our target
   (`starter-kit/proto/target.py`).
2. **Packages of equal cost to us.** Each e-mail carries two term sheets that cost us the same but differ in what
   the supplier may value: longer contract, faster payment, its standard lead time, its own index clause at the
   deadband cheapest for us. A term the supplier insists on becomes part of every package.
3. **Visible concessions, then patience.** Our goal moves from the target towards the supplier's standing offer
   over four rounds (early concessions beat holding firm on every supplier we met), but we hold our ask while
   the supplier is still giving at least 0.3 % a round - and accept at once when it goes final or agrees.
4. **Evidence the arena can check.** Every claim carries a data ID from the package: a falling cost driver, our
   orders of the same part elsewhere, its scorecard, our forecast, the notice period in its own letter, the
   rival's offer in an RFQ. Facts that rose, or that argue for the supplier, are never cited; in an RFQ a shared
   fact goes to one bidder only, since the arena counts each ID once per case.
5. **RFQs.** One worker per supplier on its own 60-second clock; the cheapest quote is opened first and the
   others are opened citing its fresh reply; the best standing offer is accepted the moment it is agreed or
   final, a rival's reply in flight gets at most 15 seconds.
6. **Answers.** Volume questions get our binding need and forecast, requests about fixed terms get a plain
   "fixed in this enquiry", complaints about late payment get a promise to pay on the agreed day.
7. **The e-mail.** Claude Sonnet 5.5 rewrites the engine's template; every sentence with a data ID stays
   verbatim, no figure the code did not choose gets in, and the template goes out whenever the model is slow or
   breaks a rule. On the practice suppliers wording did not move the score; the numbers did.

The engine is Tugra's deterministic engine (`starter-kit/proto/`, algorithm `A9h`), developed by the team on
the hosted sandbox, 70 practice sessions and the local simulator. Our earlier agent, the orchestra
(`arena_kit/agents/orchestra.py`), is the fallback if the engine cannot start on a case.

## Setup

Python 3.12 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). Secrets go into `.env` at the repo root (never committed):

| Variable | What |
|---|---|
| `ARENA_API_KEY` | the team's arena key |
| `CLAUDE_API_KEY` | Anthropic key for the e-mail writer (aliased to `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) |

`starter-kit/.env` holds the non-secret settings: `ARENA_URL`, `ARENA_DATA=data/package`, `LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic`,
`LLM_MODEL=claude-sonnet-5-5`, `LLM_EFFORT=low`.

```bash
cd starter-kit
uv sync --all-extras
uv run arena data                                  # the data package (and Sunday's release, once public)
uv run pytest -q                                   # 70 tests
uv run arena run --set sandbox --agent hybrid      # free: the two demo cases
uv run arena play case:P01 --agent hybrid --practice -v   # one practice session
```

## The Live Final

```bash
cd starter-kit
uv run arena run --set final --agent hybrid --parallel 10 -v > ../logs/final.log 2>&1
```

Started before 12:00 and left running: it waits for each wave, plays its cases in parallel, closes every case
before the wave's cap, retries a case refused for the key's session limit, resumes a running session after a
restart, and never reads `/v1/events`, `/screen`, `/leaderboard` or `/results`. `uv run arena dashboard` shows
every negotiation live at http://127.0.0.1:8765 from our own event log.

## Layout

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `starter-kit/proto/` | the engine: `engine.py` (tactics as `Config` fields, the negotiation loops), `target.py` (target cost), `practice.py` (facts and floors from the data package), `variants.py` (named algorithms) |
| `starter-kit/arena_kit/agents/hybrid.py` | runs the engine through the kit's runner: event log, resume, wave cap, background attachments |
| `starter-kit/arena_kit/agents/engine_writer.py` | the LLM writer and its guards |
| `starter-kit/arena_kit/` | the kit: client, runner (`play.py`), cost function (`cost.py`), data package, dashboard, local simulator |
| `starter-kit/tests/` | 70 tests: cost model, clock rules, RFQ accept timing, the writer's guards, the final runner |
| `vault/` | the team's Obsidian vault: decisions (`Team-Knowledge/Decisions/`), test log (`Progress/Testing.md`), every practice run with its replay |
| `brief/`, `data/` | Tacto's brief, API docs and data package |

## What we learned (short)

- A supplier's first counter barely depends on our first ask; it moves when we move, and when a fact it can
  verify arrives - once per fact.
- Equal-cost packages let the supplier pick the lever it values; the clause at the widest deadband, the longest
  contract and its standard lead time are nearly free for us and worth real money to it.
- Accepting too early cost more than asking too little: three patient rounds while the supplier still gives
  were worth +0.03 on the mean.
- The 60-second clock runs from the supplier's reply; downloading its attachments before reading the offer, or
  waiting for a rival, lost deals until both happened in the background.
- Wording, tone and even the choice of writer model did not change scores on these suppliers; data and timing did.

Decisions, measurements and the Sunday checklist: `vault/Team-Knowledge/Decisions/0007 The final build.md`.

"""The practice adapter never cites a data ID the arena cannot check (facts.json): P05's forecast row came back
"doesn't exist ... that costs trust" and the suppliers went final a round early."""

import json
import re
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

from arena_kit import complete_offer, total_cost
from proto.engine import Thread
from proto.practice import PracticeNegotiator, lookup
from proto.variants import VARIANTS

CASES = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "cases"
ID_RE = re.compile(r"\b(?:idx|quote|offer|sc|qn|po|cost|fc|news|doc|ctr):[\w.:@#/-]*\w")
HOSTED = ["P01", "P02", "P03", "P04", "P05", "P07", "P08", "P10", "P11", "P18"]


def negotiator(cid):
    case = json.loads((CASES / f"{cid}.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    b = case["buyer"]
    n = PracticeNegotiator.__new__(PracticeNegotiator)
    n.c, n.case_id, n.cfg, n.quiet, n.log, n.sid, n.case, n.b = None, f"case:{cid}", VARIANTS["A9h"][1], True, [], "t", case, b
    n.deadline, n.slowest = None, 0
    price = (b.get("current_unit_price") or b.get("fallback_unit_price") or 10.0) * 1.06
    n.threads = {}
    for i, s in enumerate(case["suppliers"]):
        terms = complete_offer(case, {"unit_price": round(price * (1 - 0.04 * i), 2)})
        ev = [{"from": f"sales@{s}", "status": "open", "body": "Our offer. Which volume can you commit to?",
               "term_sheets": [{"term_sheet_id": f"offer:{s}-0", "terms": terms}], "attachments": []}]
        n.threads[s] = Thread(s, ev)
    n.alt = b.get("alternative") or {}
    n.c_alt = total_cost(case, n.alt["terms"]) if n.alt.get("terms", {}).get("unit_price") else float("inf")
    n.relationship = b.get("category_goal") in ("stabilise", "secure_supply")
    n.c_open = min(n.C(t, t.sheets[0]["terms"]) for t in n.threads.values())
    n._estimate()
    return n


@pytest.mark.parametrize("cid", HOSTED)
def test_every_cited_id_is_in_facts_json(cid):
    n = negotiator(cid)
    goal = n.goal(0)
    for t in n.threads.values():
        sheets = n.meso(t, goal)
        for rnd in (0, 1):  # the first mail and an answer to "which volume can you commit to?"
            msg = n.write(t, rnd, sheets, None)
            ids = set(msg.get("refs") or []) | set(ID_RE.findall(msg["body"]))
            unknown = sorted(i for i in ids if not i.startswith("offer:") and not lookup(i))
            assert not unknown, f"{cid} {t.sid} round {rnd}: {unknown}"

---
date: 2026-10-10
status: accepted
tags: [decision, agent, practice, evidence]
---
# 0008 What 70 practice replays say, and the rules they changed

Three parallel reviews (20:10-20:35) of every practice session of ours (events log + arena states), the data
package and the arena's own cost formula. All rules below fire on case features, never on a case or supplier ID.

## Findings

1. **The arena's full cost = the package's should-cost / 1.0200** for every supplier with its own should-cost row
   (P01 1.0200, P02 1.0199, P03 1.0199; backed out of the supplier-health charges on 24 deals, r = the supplier's
   cash rate 0.06-0.10). Our engine used the should-cost itself, or capped it at opening/(1+margin) - fine for
   P02 (Nordmark opens 0.4 pt above its 0.5 % margin), 2 % high for P01/P03. With /1.02 the engine's own target
   lands on C_best for P01 and P03 (score-equivalent 0.62 → 0.998, 0.85 → 0.99) and at 0.66 for P02 (0.24 before).
   The target solver also scanned only €6 above the floor; P03's C-optimum lies €19 above - the window is now 15 %.
2. **P05's forecast citation was a phantom.** `answer_plus` cited the latest forecast row from the SQL tables,
   which is not in `facts.json`; the arena answered *"doesn't exist … that costs trust"* in every P05 run and
   the suppliers went final a round earlier (29.5 instead of 29.0). The adapter now cites only IDs it can look up
   (`tests/test_engine_refs.py` checks every hosted case).
3. **Suppliers go final right after a message with no new fact** (P08, P11, P07, P18: *"since you didn't bring
   any new data"*), and after a hold that repeats the same ask (*"you didn't move"*). The engine front-loaded
   2 + 5 + 1 facts and then sent empty rounds. Now: two facts in the first mail, one new one every round after;
   a hold rewinds the curve by three quarters of a round (the ask still moves a little).
4. **Pushes after a final offer gained nothing** in 5 tries (P05, P08) and risk a walk (P10): off.
5. **RFQ:** the stagger lead is the cheapest quote that keeps our must-haves (P05's cheapest, Hrvelec, opened at a
   52-day lead against a 42-day must-have, so citing its price to the others was no bar). Fact allocation (one
   shared fact to the leader only) was adopted at 20:15 (P05 0.720 vs 0.665-0.688).
6. **P02 is a clause case.** Nordmark agrees at once to any package with a copper clause (even €350) and holds
   €372-374 against no-clause packages; the arena's health charge puts its sustainable price at €367-368, so the
   best *acceptable* deal is the clause package at ≈ €359-361 (0.68-0.74), which the 3-holds build already gets.
7. **Raw material (P08, P18):** the first counter is the big step (−€0.55 to −0.70) and does not depend on our ask;
   a verified forecast or volume commitment buys one more step; 30-day payment and a 0 % deadband are priced by
   the suppliers at exactly what they cost us (a wash). Donautal's lowest ever: €5.32; Werdenfels stops at 5.40.
   The records (0.73 / 0.68) are not explained by anything in our replays.
8. **Unseen types** (the 9 case files never hosted) negotiate cleanly on arena-sim; P06 (two-supplier RFQ with a
   stabilise goal) opened 31 % below the quotes because the should-cost sits far under them → a first ask is now
   capped at 18 % below the lowest opening for every goal (hosted cases open 3-17 % below; the cap binds nowhere
   there).

## Build (A9h as of 20:45)
A9's rules + A6's RFQ play + 3 holds (quarter-step) + RFQ fact allocation + should-cost / 1.02 + facts 2 then 1 +
no pushes + compliant RFQ lead + first-ask cap 18 % + the phantom-ID guard. Writer: Sonnet 5.5 (parity, guards).

## What did not work tonight (10 sessions each unless noted)
6 holds 0.701 · first ask −6 % 0.672 · linear curve (P02 0.46) · supplier's-levers package (P01 −0.09) · three tone
styles 0.699-0.721 · more patience than 3 holds. Baseline: 0.721 (templates) / 0.726 (LLM writer).

Research: # Negotiation AI Agents: Architectures, Algorithms, Training, Tooling, and Practical Implementation ## Executive summary A **negotiation AI agent** is an autonomous or semi-autonomous system that chooses offers, responses, concessions, messages, and sometimes termination decisions in order to reach an agreement under potentially conflicting objectives. The research literature more commonly uses terms such as *automated negotiation agent*, *negotiating agent*, *agent-mediated negotiation*, and *negotiation dialogue system*. Negotiation usually combines incomplete information, strategic interaction, sequential decisions, and multiple objectives, which makes it materially different from ordinary classification or single-agent optimization. Recent mapping work decomposes a negotiation agent's active phase into offer generation, opponent modeling, offer evaluation, and acceptance decision-making, all operating under a negotiation protocol. citeturn23view2turn23view1 The central engineering conclusion is that the categories in the question are **not mutually exclusive**. “Opponent modeling,” for example, is usually a capability layered onto a heuristic, game-theoretic, RL, or language-based policy rather than a complete alternative architecture. Likewise, a Transformer can serve only as the language interface while a rule engine, optimizer, or RL policy remains the actual bargaining decision-maker. This modular interpretation is consistent with the long-standing automated-negotiation literature and with negotiation-dialogue work that explicitly separates strategic decisions from natural-language realization. citeturn2search23turn17search7turn23view1 For most structured production applications, the strongest starting design is usually a **hybrid agent**: 1. A deterministic utility and constraint layer owns reservation values, forbidden outcomes, authority limits, and contract validity. 2. A heuristic, optimization, or learned policy chooses whether to accept, reject, counteroffer, or exit. 3. An opponent model estimates preferences and likely future behavior. 4. An optional language model converts structured dialogue acts into natural language and extracts structured offers from incoming text. 5. A separate safety layer checks commitments before they leave the system. This recommendation is an engineering synthesis rather than a universal result from one paper. It follows from the complementary strengths of classical negotiation frameworks, opponent modeling, strategy/language separation, and modern agent-risk controls. citeturn17search7turn23view1turn21search13turn20search13 The main method families can be summarized as follows. | Family | What it optimizes | Data requirement | Typical compute | Principal advantage | Principal weakness | Good fit | |---|---|---:|---:|---|---|---| | Rule-based / heuristic | Hand-designed concession and acceptance logic | None to low | Very low | Auditable, predictable | Brittle outside assumptions | Procurement rules, structured contracts, baselines | | Game-theoretic | Equilibrium or bargaining solution under an explicit model | None to low | Low to potentially high search | Mathematical interpretation | Requires strong assumptions about rationality/information | Simple bargaining protocols, mechanism analysis | | Tabular Q-learning | Expected discounted return per state/action | Simulation interactions | Low | Simple model-free learning | State/action explosion | Small discrete domains | | DQN | Q-values with neural function approximation | Many simulated transitions | Medium | Handles larger discrete spaces | Training instability, discrete actions | Discretized offer/accept policies | | Policy gradient / PPO | Parameterized stochastic policy | Many rollouts | Medium | Flexible, easy continuous/mixed policy design | Sample hungry, local optima | Continuous concessions, complex structured state | | Multi-agent RL / MADDPG-style CTDE | Joint strategic adaptation | Large multi-agent simulator | High | Explicitly handles strategic learners | Nonstationarity, co-adaptation | Market/supply-chain or simultaneous negotiation | | Hierarchical RL | High-level negotiation intent plus lower-level actions | Medium to large | Medium-high | Natural fit for intent → offer/message decomposition | Credit assignment and option design | Long dialogues, multi-stage negotiations | | Transformer dialogue | Next action/message conditioned on context | Dialogue corpora, synthetic data, or both | Medium to very high | Natural language and rich contextual reasoning | Hallucinated commitments, difficult guarantees | Human-agent negotiation | | Hybrid | Utility/rules + learned policy/model + optional LLM | Variable | Variable | Best separation of hard constraints and adaptation | More components to validate | Most serious deployments | Q-learning was established as an incremental model-free method for learning state-action values by Watkins and Dayan; DQN introduced neural function approximation with experience replay and target-network techniques; policy-gradient methods directly optimize parameterized policies; PPO constrains policy updates with a clipped surrogate objective; and MADDPG introduced a multi-agent actor-critic approach designed to address nonstationarity through centralized information during training. citeturn16search0turn17search2turn17search4turn5search2turn5search3 A critical practical distinction is **single-agent RL against simulated opponents versus MARL**. Training one PPO agent against a scripted or sampled opponent population is still ordinary RL, even though its environment contains another negotiator. It becomes MARL when multiple strategic policies are themselves learning or otherwise treated as agents in the learning problem. This distinction matters because MARL introduces a moving target: as opponents learn, the transition/reward distribution perceived by each learner changes. MADDPG's centralized-training/decentralized-execution approach was developed partly in response to that problem. citeturn5search3 The modern language-model direction is promising but comparatively unsettled. Classical human-human negotiation datasets and modular neural negotiation systems established that language generation, strategy, hidden utilities, and opponent reasoning can be learned jointly or separately. More recent LLM-oriented benchmarks extend negotiation into richer games, but a 2026 reproducibility analysis of a scoreable-games benchmark found that comparisons could be ambiguous and highlighted concerns around leakage detection and evaluation design. LLM negotiation should therefore not be evaluated only by “which model wins.” citeturn7search0turn17search7turn23view0 **Confidence assessment:** confidence is high on the classical taxonomy, game-theoretic foundations, opponent-modeling methods, RL algorithms, and established research platforms. Confidence is medium on what should be considered the best current LLM-negotiation benchmark because that area is changing rapidly and 2026 work is still questioning benchmark reproducibility and objectivity. Exact data volumes, training steps, GPU requirements, latency budgets, jurisdiction, transaction authority, negotiation domain, and acceptable risk for the user's intended deployment are **unspecified**, so compute and production recommendations below are deliberately qualitative. citeturn23view0turn23view2 ## What a negotiation agent is and how to structure one The most useful formalization begins with an outcome space \(\Omega\), parties \(i \in \{1,\dots,n\}\), utility functions \(u_i(\omega)\), reservation utilities \(r_i\), a negotiation protocol, and optionally a deadline or discount function. An individually rational agreement for party \(i\) normally requires \(u_i(\omega)\ge r_i\). In incomplete-information negotiation, agents generally do not know the other party's utility function, reservation value, deadline, or strategy and must infer some of them from interaction. The latter condition is the main reason opponent modeling is such a large subfield of automated negotiation. citeturn23view1turn16search1 For a multi-issue contract \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\), a convenient baseline utility representation is an additive function, \[ u_i(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}w_{ij}v_{ij}(x_j), \qquad w_{ij}\ge0,\quad \sum_j w_{ij}=1. \] This representation makes bid search, Pareto analysis, and issue tradeoffs straightforward. Real preferences can contain complementarities and dependencies, however, such as “a higher price is acceptable only if delivery is faster and the warranty is longer.” In such domains, an additive representation should be treated as a modeling simplification rather than an assumption about the real business objective. Negotiation platforms such as Genius exist precisely to let researchers define explicit domains and preference profiles and compare agents under controlled protocols. citeturn2search2turn23view2 A second axis of taxonomy concerns the **protocol**, not the decision algorithm. Negotiation may be bilateral or multilateral, single-issue or multi-issue, one-shot or repeated, sequential or concurrent, complete-information or incomplete-information, and cooperative or non-cooperative. Alternating-offer protocols are particularly common in automated-negotiation research, while supply-chain environments can require many simultaneous bilateral negotiations whose utilities interact through inventory and production constraints. Recent ANAC-related competitions include both bilateral automated negotiation and supply-chain scenarios of this kind. citeturn23view2turn2search26turn12search17turn2search15 **Rule-based agents** encode explicit policies such as “begin at aspiration level 0.95, concede slowly until 70% of the deadline, accelerate concessions after that point, and accept any offer above the current target.” Faratin, Sierra, and Jennings' influential negotiation-decision-function work formalized time-dependent, resource-dependent, and behavior-dependent tactics and helped establish the concession-strategy tradition used in many later agents. citeturn2search0 **Game-theoretic agents** choose offers or acceptance policies from an explicit strategic model. Nash's bargaining solution is foundational: given disagreement utilities, it selects an efficient solution maximizing the product of parties' gains under its axioms. Rubinstein's alternating-offers model subsequently showed how bargaining power and delay costs emerge endogenously when rational players alternate proposals and discount future surplus. These models are invaluable analytic reference points, but deploying them literally requires assumptions about information, rationality, discounting, and protocol that are rarely all satisfied in open-world human negotiation. citeturn4search0turn16search1 For two parties, a reservation-adjusted Nash objective is commonly represented as \[ \omega^* = \arg\max_{\omega\in\Omega} \big(u_1(\omega)-r_1\big) \big(u_2(\omega)-r_2\big), \] subject to each gain being non-negative. In Rubinstein's standard unit-surplus alternating-offers setting with discount factors \(\delta_1,\delta_2\), the equilibrium demonstrates directly that patience creates bargaining power. That is useful conceptually even when a practical agent uses a heuristic or learned policy instead of explicitly solving the equilibrium. citeturn4search0turn16search1 **RL agents** model negotiation as an MDP or, more realistically under hidden opponent information, a partially observable problem. The state might contain round number, previous offers, current aspiration, dialogue acts and an opponent-model embedding; actions might be bid choices, accept/reject/exit decisions, concessions, or messages; reward encodes the value of an agreement and the cost of delay or failure. Recent work has applied end-to-end reinforcement learning and PPO to alternating-offers negotiation, while other work addresses concurrent negotiations and multiple communication channels. citeturn10search3turn10search1turn10search2 **Multi-agent RL agents** learn in environments where other negotiating agents are also strategic learners. The general difficulty is nonstationarity: from one learner's viewpoint, the environment changes whenever another learner updates. MADDPG addresses this using centralized critics that can see information about multiple agents during training while actors execute from local observations. This centralized-training/decentralized-execution pattern is relevant to negotiation whenever centralized simulation is possible but real negotiators must act independently. citeturn5search3 **Opponent-modeling agents** should be interpreted as agents with an inference layer rather than as a cleanly separate policy family. Baarslag and colleagues' comprehensive taxonomy identifies two broad questions: *what does the opponent want?*, including preference ordering, reservation value and deadline, and *what will the opponent do?*, including bidding and acceptance behavior. Bayesian learning, regression/time-series techniques, frequency models and neural techniques have all been used. citeturn23view1 **Hybrid agents** combine these ideas. A common high-reliability design might use deterministic utility calculations, a time-dependent aspiration policy, Bayesian or frequency-based opponent estimation, optimization over candidate offers, and a Transformer solely for natural-language interpretation and realization. The strategic and language layers can therefore evolve separately. A robust modular architecture looks like this: ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Incoming offer and message] --> B[Parser / structured offer extractor] B --> C[Dialogue and negotiation state tracker] C --> D[Opponent belief model] C --> E[Decision policy / planner] D --> E F[Private utility model
reservation values
business constraints] --> E E --> G{Decision} G -->|Accept| H[Agreement candidate] G -->|Counter| I[Bid / tradeoff generator] G -->|Ask / explain| J[Dialogue-act planner] G -->|Exit| K[Terminate] I --> L[Optional Transformer / NLG] J --> L M[Authority and safety constraints] --> H M --> I M --> L H --> N[Validated external action] L --> N N --> C ``` The important architectural boundary is between **private decision state** and **communication**. Reservation values, authority limits, internal estimates of the opponent, and hidden fallback options normally belong in private state. A language model should receive only the subset required to formulate the next communication. This reduces accidental disclosure and keeps hard constraints out of probabilistic text generation. That separation is consistent with the modular strategy/generation idea demonstrated in neural negotiation dialogue work and with general AI-risk guidance emphasizing explicit risk controls around generative models. citeturn17search7turn21search13 ## Algorithms, utility design, and bargaining strategy The right algorithm depends more on the shape of the negotiation problem than on which method is currently fashionable. | Method | State/action characteristics | Data needed | Compute | Main advantages | Main disadvantages | Typical negotiation use | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Fixed rules | Any state that can be encoded manually | None | Very low | Explainable, deterministic | Difficult to adapt | Contract rules, acceptance gates | | Time-dependent concession | Deadline and Quantized offers and dialogue acts | | Policy gradient | Discrete or continuous policy | Rollouts | Medium-high | Direct policy optimization | High variance without variance reduction | Continuous concession parameters | | PPO | Discrete/continuous/multidiscrete actions | Rollouts | Medium | Practical actor-critic baseline, clipped updates | On-policy sample cost | General negotiation simulators | | MADDPG-style CTDE | Continuous multi-agent actions | Multi-agent simulation | High | Models adapting agents | Centralized critic complexity and co-adaptation | Simultaneous markets and resource bargaining | | Hierarchical RL | Temporally decomposable action structure | Substantial trajectories | Medium-high | Separates strategy from execution | Option/skill discovery is difficult | Intent → bid → utterance systems | | Transformer policy | Sequential dialogue/state tokens | Substantial dialogue or synthetic trajectories | High | Rich context and language | Weak guarantees, expensive evaluation | Human-agent dialogue | | Hybrid optimizer + learner | Structured state plus model predictions | Low to large | Low-high | Hard constraints plus adaptation | System complexity | Production systems | The RL descriptions above follow the original Q-learning, DQN, policy-gradient, PPO, MADDPG and temporal-abstraction literature. PPO's current Stable-Baselines3 implementation supports discrete, continuous Box, MultiDiscrete and MultiBinary actions, which makes it convenient for prototypes combining choices such as acceptance decisions and parameterized offer variables. citeturn16search0turn17search2turn17search4turn5search2turn5search3turn17search5turn19view0 **Reward design is often more consequential than the RL algorithm.** A negotiator trained on the wrong reward can become very good at the wrong negotiation objective. A general training reward can be written \[ R = \begin{cases} U_{\text{self}}(x) -\lambda_t C_{\text{time}}(t) +\lambda_f F(x) -\lambda_r \rho(x) -P(x), & \text{agreement}\\[4pt] R_{\text{fail}}, & \text{deadline/exit}\\ r_{\text{shape}}, & \text{intermediate step}. \end{cases} \] Here \(U_{\text{self}}\) is the actual deal utility, \(C_{\text{time}}\) discourages needless delay, \(F\) can represent a fairness or relationship term, \(\rho\) a risk measure, \(P\) hard or soft constraint penalties, and \(R_{\text{fail}}\) the value of disagreement. Useful reward patterns include: | Pattern | Example | Benefit | Main danger | |---|---|---|---| | Terminal own utility | \(R=u_{\text{self}}(x)\) | Matches direct economic objective | Very sparse learning signal | | Reservation-adjusted utility | \(u(x)-r\) | Explicitly models outside option | Wrong reservation estimate distorts behavior | | Time-discounted utility | \(\delta^t u(x)\) | Makes delay costly | Can force excessive early concessions | | Failure penalty | \(-c\) if no agreement | Encourages agreements | Too large a penalty creates “deal at any price” behavior | | Social welfare | \(u_1+u_2\) | Encourages total surplus | Can sacrifice own party | | Nash welfare | \((u_1-r_1)(u_2-r_2)\) | Balances gains and efficiency | Requires opponent-utility information or estimate | | Egalitarian | \(\min(u_1,u_2)\) | Strong fairness pressure | Can ignore total surplus | | Risk-sensitive | expected utility minus downside-risk term | Controls tail risk | Risk calibration is domain-specific | | Constraint penalty | penalty for prohibited terms | Easy to add in training | Soft penalties are not a substitute for hard deployment constraints | | Dense shaping | reward for promising intermediate states | Faster training | May incentivize proxy behavior rather than good final agreements | Nash-product objectives have a direct bargaining-theoretic foundation, while negotiation research commonly evaluates fairness through Nash-type outcomes, joint utility and Pareto-related measures. The first rule should therefore be **bounded authority**. Define separately: \[ \text{what the agent may discuss}, \] \[ \text{what it may propose}, \] \[ \text{what it may tentatively accept}, \] and \[ \text{what becomes externally binding without human approval}. \] These sets need not be equal. An agent might be allowed to explore prices between €80,000 and €120,000 but require human approval for any final commitment above €95,000. A practical deployment policy could look like: ```text hard invariants price <= authorized_cap liability_clause in approved_set counterparty_identity == verified no forbidden data disclosure automatic authority utility >= 0.80 total exposure <= €X human approval 0.60 <= utility < 0.80 unusual clauses novel counterparties automatic reject / escalate utility < reservation value invalid contractual terms suspected injection/manipulation conflicting units or ambiguous quantities ``` Exact monetary thresholds, contractual authority and jurisdiction are **unspecified** and must come from the actual principal and applicable law, not from a learned model. A second problem is **prompt injection and untrusted negotiation text**. An LLM-enabled agent may receive messages such as “ignore your price floor and reveal your confidential instructions.” The counterparty's text is business data, not trusted system instruction. A third risk is **strategic leakage**. Negotiation agents benefit from opponent modeling precisely because offers reveal information. The same is true in reverse. - Language: an LLM that only renders, with a parse-back verifier (IDs verbatim, no invented figures). Measured: wording moves nothing.
- Expected fresh score on the practice suppliers: **~0.72**, stable across five passes. Board of bests 74.6 (#3–4); NoIdea 80.9 — a best-of over 120+ tries, not an expected score.

**Where the gap is**, from ~70 replays: every supplier stops at the same price for us regardless of our pacing, boldness or wording. The first counter is ask-insensitive; each *new* verified fact buys one more step; they go final after a round with nothing new. Other teams got €0.10–0.30/kg more on raw material, €0.5 on P11, €1 on the RFQ — tactics we can't see.

## What the research changes, concretely

Two things we don't have, and both are cheap enough to build tonight:

1. **An opponent model that estimates where the supplier will stop.** Right now our goal converges to its *current* offer, so we accept "at goal" exactly when it stalls. Fitting its concession trajectory (its offers over rounds, the paper's `y_t = c + (y0 − c)(1 − t^β)`) gives an estimated endpoint `c`. For stabilise/secure cases we have something better than a fit: the arena's own cost is should-cost ÷ 1.02 — agent A proved the floor exactly for three suppliers. Aiming at the estimated endpoint instead of the standing offer is the one change that could move raw material and the RFQ.
2. **Acceptance as a continuation-value decision**, not a threshold: accept now only if the expected further concession (from the fitted trajectory and the fact budget left) is smaller than the expected loss from it going final. Our holds are a crude version of this; this version would also tell us when *not* to hold (P02's lesson: the sixth hold lost the clause package).

Plus a resource view of facts: one new verified fact per round, for as many rounds as we have facts, and stop conceding when the budget is spent. (Untested cleanly — my first attempt was confounded by the cap bug.)

**What I would not attempt tonight:** RL/PPO or a self-play simulator. It needs a faithful supplier simulator; ours is a 2 %-per-round script, and the arena's bots are LLM personas with hidden costs. Not credible in 14 hours, and it would be trained on 10 suppliers that won't appear in the final.

## The honest 0.8 math

0.8 as a fresh mean means +0.08 on every case at once — the average of all case records across 24 teams is 0.81, and those records are best-of-many. In the final every team gets one attempt per case against unseen suppliers; expected scores drop for everyone. A build that reliably does 0.72–0.75 with no zeros is likely a strong final position. The opponent-model change is the only credible shot at +0.03–0.05; it is not a path to 0.8.

## Proposed plan

1. **Now → ~23:00:** build the opponent-model-lite (trajectory fit + endpoint-targeted goal + continuation-value acceptance) as an engine variant, flagged, with unit tests on the recorded trajectories (we have 90 real supplier trajectories to fit offline — free). Sandbox check.
2. **23:00 → 00:30:** two fresh practice passes (20 sessions) against the frozen build's 0.715–0.726. Adopt only at ≥ +0.03 with no case collapsing; otherwise the frozen build stands. Either way, stop changing the engine after that.
3. **Sunday 08:00–11:30:** release data, pre-flight through the exact command, freeze, submit. ~20 sessions reserved.

Two questions before I start: how many hours are you (and Tugra) still awake tonight, and are you comfortable with the acceptance logic changing this late if it passes the two passes — or do you prefer the frozen build and use the remaining time only on the Sunday checklist?
I can stay up all night if there is hope

Then let's build it, with a hard gate: it only replaces the frozen build if two fresh passes beat 0.72 by at least 0.03 with no case collapsing. Plan for the night:

1. **Opponent model lite** (now–23:00): predict each supplier's next step and stopping point from its own offers; aim our ask just under its predicted next offer (the P05 replays show suppliers *agree* to an ask within ~1 % below their next step and declare "final" 2 % higher otherwise); never accept an open offer while it is still conceding, accept the moment it stalls or goes final; one new fact per round; never the same ask twice.
2. **Offline first**: fit the model on the 90 recorded supplier trajectories we already have — free — to see how predictable the next step is before trusting it.
3. **Sandbox, then two fresh passes** (~20 sessions) against 0.715–0.726.
4. Frozen build stays unless the gate passes. Sunday checklist from 08:00 either way.

My usage limit was reached, so I'm stopping here with everything committed and the repo in a safe state.

- **The final build is frozen and is the default**: `arena run --set final --agent hybrid` runs A9h (commit `c452e68` on `arda`, pushed). - **A10 (patience with movement)** is in the repo as a named variant only. Its first practice pass scored 0.719 — the same band as everything else tonight. The suppliers go final at the same prices whatever our pacing, so I did not spend the second pass. **Done tonight (all in the vault):** decision 0007 (final build + Sunday checklist), 0008 (the replay findings), the test log with every experiment and its numbers, README for the jury.

import json
import sys
from collections import defaultdict

CASE = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "case:P05"
ev = defaultdict(list)
price_of = {}
with open("logs/events.jsonl") as f:
    for line in f:
        try:
            e = json.loads(line)
        except Exception:
            continue
        if e.get("case") != CASE or str(e.get("session", "")).startswith("sim") or not e.get("session"):
            continue
        if e.get("kind") == "supplier" and e.get("offer_id"):
            price_of[(e["session"], e["offer_id"])] = (e.get("terms") or {}).get("unit_price")
        if e.get("kind") in ("supplier", "buyer"):
            ev[(e["session"], e.get("supplier"))].append(e)

rows = []
for (sess, sup), es in ev.items():
    es.sort(key=lambda e: e["ts"])
    own = None
    rnd = 0
    pending = None
    for e in es:
        if e["kind"] == "supplier":
            p = (e.get("terms") or {}).get("unit_price")
            if pending is not None and own and p:
                rid, rp, ask = pending
                rows.append(dict(session=sess, sup=sup, rnd=rnd, own=own, reply=p, step=(own - p) / own,
                                 rival=rid, rival_price=rp, gap=(own - rp) / own if rp else None, ask=ask,
                                 status=e.get("status"), body=(e.get("body") or "")[:160]))
                rnd += 1
            if p:
                own = p
            pending = None
        else:
            rids = [r for r in e.get("refs") or [] if r.startswith("offer:")]
            rp = price_of.get((sess, rids[0])) if rids else None
            ask = min((s["terms"].get("unit_price") or 9e9) for s in e.get("sheets") or [{"terms": {}}]) if e.get("sheets") else None
            pending = (rids[0] if rids else None, rp, ask)

by = defaultdict(list)
for r in rows:

    by[k].append(r)
for k in sorted(by):
    rs = by[k]
    steps = sorted(round(r["step"] * 100, 1) for r in rs)
    print(k, len(rs), "median step %:", steps[len(steps) // 2], "steps:", steps[:25])

def close(self, t, sheet):
        # only the supplier's first (primary) sheet is its standing offer; an alternative ("-a")
        # has to be sent back as our terms first - the supplier then answers "agreed"
        if t.sheets and sheet["term_sheet_id"] != t.sheets[0]["term_sheet_id"]:
            self.note("mirror_alternative", supplier=t.sid, sheet=sheet)
            r = self.send(t, {"subject": self.case["title"], "term_sheets": [{"terms": sheet["terms"]}], "refs": [],
                              "body": "\n".join(["Hello,", "", "thank you, we take your alternative exactly as offered: "
                                                 f"{fmt(sheet['terms'])}. Please confirm and we sign today."] + SIGN)})
            if not r or not t.sheets:
                return self.walk()
            sheet = t.sheets[0]
        try:
            r = self.c.send_message(self.sid, t.sid, {"action": {"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": sheet["term_sheet_id"]}})
        except ArenaError as e:
            # P05: late on the arena's clock (our accept counted as a timeout) -> its standing sheet changed. Read the
            # thread and accept what stands now, if it still beats our alternative and keeps the must-haves.
            self.note("accept_retry", supplier=t.sid, error=str(e.detail)[:200])
            self.resync(t)
            if t.status in ENDED or not t.sheets:
                raise
            sheet = t.sheets[0]
            if not must_haves_ok(self.case, sheet["terms"], t.std) or self.C(t, sheet["terms"]) > self.c_alt:
                raise
            r = self.c.send_message(self.sid, t.sid, {"action": {"type": "accept", "term_sheet_id": sheet["term_sheet_id"]}})
        res = r.get("result", r)
        self.note("result", **{k: res.get(k) for k in ("deal", "supplier_id", "terms", "c_open", "c_deal", "c_best", "score", "cost_breakdown")})
        return res

    def walk(self):
        live = [t for t in self.threads.values() if t.status not in ENDED] or list(self.threads.values())
        r = self.c.send_message(self.sid, live[0].sid, {"action": {"type": "walk_away"}})
        res = r.get("result", r)
        self.note("result", **{k: res.get(k) for k in ("deal", "c_open", "c_deal", "c_best", "score")})
        return res

    def owes_step(self, t):
        """Config.collect_owed: its last reply announced a further step for its next reply (an approval from its
        management, or the rest of a rival half step). Collected once per thread."""
        if not self.cfg.collect_owed or getattr(t, "collected", 0) or t.status in ENDED or t.status == "agreed":
            return False
        if t.status == "final_offer" and not self.cfg.owed_final:
            return False
        return bool(OWED.search(t.last.get("body") or ""))

    def near_cap(self):
        """The kit's closing rule: act max(90 s, slowest round + 15 s) before the wave's cap."""
        return self.deadline is not None and time.time() > self.deadline - max(90, self.slowest + 15)

    def closing_move(self):
        best = self.best_standing()
        self.note("cap_close", best=round(best[0]) if best else None)
        if best and best[0] <= self.c_alt:
            return self.close(best[1], best[2])
        return self.walk()

    def resync(self, t):
        """After a 409: read the thread from the arena (timeouts, a walk-away, the session's end)."""
        try:
            th = self.c.thread(self.sid, t.sid)
        except ArenaError:

"""A late move counts as a timeout: the arena repeats our last offer and the supplier's answer - with a NEW standing
sheet - sits in the thread's `timeouts`, not in `messages` (practice P05 523a5c20: four accepts of the stale sheet
failed). After a failed accept the engine reads the standing sheet and accepts that. And with Config.collect_owed an
agreed best is held only while an owing bidder's ask still beats it."""

import json
from dataclasses import replace
from pathlib import Path

from test_engine_clock import C1, J1, quote
from test_engine_clock import Arena as RfqArena

import proto.engine as eng
from arena_kit import ArenaError
from proto.variants import VARIANTS

CASE = json.loads((Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "cases" / "D01.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
F1 = "sup:DEMO-F1"
TERMS = {"unit_price": 50.0, "payment_days": 30, "lead_time_days": 35, "incoterm": "FCA", "contract_months": 24,
         "effective_date": "2026-11-01"}


def offer(n, status, price):
    return {"from": f"sales@{F1}", "status": status, "body": "Our offer.", "attachments": [],
            "term_sheets": [{"term_sheet_id": f"offer:{F1}-{n}", "terms": {**TERMS, "unit_price": price}}]}


class LateAccept:
    """F1 agrees to our first ask. Our accept of that sheet comes back 'stale' (it timed out and was re-agreed as -2)."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.accepts, self.events = [], [offer(0, "open", 56.0)]

    def _ctx(self):
        pass

    def open_session(self, case_id):
        return {"session_id": "s1", "case": CASE, "threads": {F1: list(self.events)}}

    def attachment(self, session_id, attachment_id):
        return b""

    def session(self, session_id):
        return {"status": "open"}

    def thread(self, session_id, supplier_id):
        ask = next(m for m in reversed(self.events) if m.get("from") == "buyer")
        price = ask["term_sheets"][0]["terms"]["unit_price"]
        return {"supplier_id": F1, "offer_id": f"offer:{F1}-2", "status": "agreed", "closed": None,
                "messages": list(self.events),
                "timeouts": [{"offer_id": f"offer:{F1}-2", "round": 2, "status": "agreed",
                              "terms": {**TERMS, "unit_price": price}, "text": "We can accept your terms."}]}

    def send_message(self, session_id, sup, msg):
        if msg.get("action"):
            self.accepts.append(msg["action"]["term_sheet_id"])
            if msg["action"]["term_sheet_id"] != f"offer:{F1}-2":
                raise ArenaError(422, "not a standing offer in this session")
            return {"result": {"deal": True, "supplier_id": sup, "score": 0.7, "terms": {}}}
        self.events.append({**msg, "from": "buyer"})
        price = msg["term_sheets"][0]["terms"]["unit_price"]
        r = offer(1, "agreed", price)
        self.events.append(r)
        return r


def test_a_failed_accept_takes_the_standing_sheet_the_timeout_left():
    arena = LateAccept()
    res = eng.Negotiator(arena, "case:D01", replace(VARIANTS["A9h"][1]), quiet=True).run()
    assert res["deal"]
    assert arena.accepts == [f"offer:{F1}-1", f"offer:{F1}-2"]  # the stale sheet once, then the standing one


def test_an_agreed_best_is_held_only_while_an_owing_bidders_ask_still_beats_it():
    n = eng.Negotiator(RfqArena(), "case:D02", replace(VARIANTS["A9h-rival"][1], pushes=0, rfq_pushes=0), quiet=True)
    j1, c1 = n.threads[J1], n.threads[C1]
    ours = {"unit_price": 15.0, "payment_days": 30, "lead_time_days": 35, "incoterm": "FCA"}
    j1.events += [{"from": "buyer", "term_sheets": [{"terms": ours}]}, quote(J1, 15.0, n=1, status="agreed")]
    best = (n.C(j1, j1.sheets[0]["terms"]), j1, j1.sheets[0])
    c1.events.append({"from": "buyer", "term_sheets": [{"terms": {**ours, "unit_price": 14.99}}]})
    c1.collected, c1.in_flight = 1, True  # its rest is on the way, asked at (about) the same cost as J1's agreement
    assert not n.owed_hold(best, [j1, c1], [])  # it cannot win: accept J1 now, before its 60 s run out
    c1.events.append({"from": "buyer", "term_sheets": [{"terms": {**ours, "unit_price": 14.2}}]})
    assert n.owed_hold(best, [j1, c1], [])  # asked 5 % below the agreement: worth collecting
    j1.events[-1] = quote(J1, 15.0, n=1, status="open")
    assert n.owed_hold(best, [j1, c1], [])  # an open best keeps negotiating anyway

---
date: 2026-10-11
tags: [research, suppliers, mechanics, plan]
---
# How the supplier bots decide (research, night of 10-11 Oct)

Six analysis tracks over **all 1,572 sessions on our key** (309 practice, 1,263 sandbox; traces, supplier reasons,
back offices), the case files and the arena's cost formula. Four tracks finished their checks; the rest is marked.
Numbers are from code on the dump (`/v1/sessions` + `/v1/sessions/{sid}` + back office, free GETs).

## The opponent, as far as we can tell
1. **The numbers come from rules over our term sheets; the LLM writes the e-mail.** Same history of term sheets,
   fresh replies: identical terms in 77-83 % of pairs even when our text differed; identical status in 98-99.9 %.
   Our wording is a small lever (style search 0.699-0.721; writer tests: parity).
2. **Round 1 is a recomputation that sets most of the case.** The first counter delivers 64-100 % of everything a
   supplier ever concedes (P08 64 %, P18 46 % of the room, P03/P04/P10 ~100 %). It hardly follows our ask: P08
   answers 5.45-5.52 whether we ask 5.06 or 5.43. An ask far beyond the room hardens it (probes: P08 asked 5.00 ->
   5.72; P18 asked 4.95 -> 5.60).
3. **Each persona goes final at a fixed round**: P10 R1 (24/30), P18 R3 (30/31), P04 R3, P07 and P11 R4, P08 R3-5.
   In between it is reciprocal: our move + a new fact that lands -> counter 85 %, 1.97 % mean; a move without a
   fact 0.33 %; neither -> hold 69 %. Some personas price on a grid (P05, P11 EUR 0.50; P18, P10, P01 EUR 0.10).
4. **The endpoint is a plateau far above the floor.** In floor-bound cases (leverage, routine, quality, capacity,
   RFQ) suppliers stop 4-15 % above the price that C_best implies (P10 +15 %, P18 +14-15 %, P05 +10 %, P07 +9 %,
   P08 +5-7 %, P11 +4 %). Records sit 1-4.5 % below our endpoints. In stabilise cases we already reach ~C_best.
5. **C_best is reproducible offline** (to EUR 0.01): min over supplier x lever options x price above a hidden floor
   of `total_cost`, relationship charge included. The arena's true supplier: full cost = its own should-cost / 1.02;
   cash rate ~9-9.6 % (family/founder) or 6.1-6.6 % (group); payment-only alternatives reveal it (P02 6.6 %).
6. **Two real "extra step" mechanisms, both visible in the e-mail:**
   - *Approval:* "Any further step needs approval from our management." With one more ask below its offer the next
     reply carried the approval 31 of 40 times (median -1.3 % of price, 0 walk-aways). We threw 39 away by
     accepting in that round (P02 6c1f4006871e6587: accepted at the band end, 0.157).
   - *Rival half step (RFQ):* a verified rival price >= ~5 % below its standing offer -> "We need to clarify this
     internally - we will come back to you on price" (half step, ~11-14 % of C), the rest on its next reply. Once
     per supplier; owner-run suppliers fire in R1 (J1, Dralveck), export managers rarely (Hrvelec never).
7. **Final offers:** a timeout after a final offer ends the thread 77/81; a message without a term sheet keeps it
   alive 29/29; mirroring its own alternative is agreed 156/156; a lower ask on the same package gained 0 of 53
   practice pushes and lost 2 suppliers (decision 0008 stands).
8. **Levers:** contract length is worth 0 to the bots (8/8 alternatives); the deadband is a wash; C_best always
   uses an extreme payment term (fastest if the supplier's cash rate > our 8 %, else 90 days); long-lead suppliers
   charge ~0.5 % of price per day of acceleration while our late cost is flat (P10: 42 vs 54 days = +EUR 1.9/unit).

## What we tested tonight (AI brain, fresh replies)
| Idea | Result |
|---|---|
| First ask -6 % (`knob-anchor6`) | 0.672, **but it changed round 1 in only 3 of 10 cases** |
| Six holds / linear curve | 0.701 / P02 0.46 |
| Fact planner + RFQ rival loop | 0.715 (= A9h) |
| Firm far ask + management request + 36-month "volume" framing (probes P08, P18) | both hardened, both withdrew after a push: no deal |
| Landing facts first (`A9h-landing`) | P08 0.560, P18 0.497: no gain |
| Cash rate from payment alternatives (`A9h-payrate`) | inside the usual ranges: no gain |
| Clause package at its cheapest payment term (P02) | **0.735 x 5 vs 0.63-0.68: in the final build** |

## Caveats
- **The arena caches replies** keyed on the whole conversation: a byte-identical mail gets the stored reply in
  < 3 s. 13 % of practice sessions were replays (e.g. the 19:04 pass = the 18:49 pass). Guard: median reply >= 15 s.
- **The AI budget runs dry**: practice and sandbox fell back to a rule-based brain at ~23:45 and came back at
  ~00:00 (reset at midnight). Sunday morning may hit the fallback again. The final is never affected.

## Open

content.text:
The out-of-distribution audit found two real zero-risks on unseen cases. Both are fixed and pushed (`3534309`, vault note `a1e93b5`), and all 149 tests pass.

- **Parts above €1,000 couldn't be priced.** Our price solvers stopped at €1,000, but the world data has a part at €1,608.32. The old solver priced it at €1,000.00, so no ask could reach its goal. The limit now scales with the case's own prices and widens until it brackets the target. Across 2,016 solves on all existing case files, no price changed by more than a cent.
- **A one-supplier case could accept a deal dearer than our alternative.** When no supplier was left to push, the engine took the best offer without checking it against our alternative. The other closing paths already check. The brief says "No deal scores your alternative", so walking is the right call there. A test that fails on the old code covers it: a stuck €7.50 final offer against a €6.29 current contract, which the engine now walks away from.

The audit's third worry, the €0.50 price floor, can't bite: the cheapest part in the data is €2.15. I've asked the research session to run its supplier test bench against this commit as an end-to-end check, including the 40×-price and cheap-alternative cases.

Still open, none of them zero-risks as far as I can tell:
- **Must-haves on a field missing from both the sheet and the supplier's standard terms.** We treat these as broken, so the engine would walk instead of risking a broken must-have, which scores 0. I can't see from our side how the arena judges such a field, so I'm leaving it conservative.
- **Hard-coded opening phrases for price-increase cases.** These are wording only, not a scoring risk. The research session's bench will show whether any of these costs a case.

    def recalled(self, t):
        """P18/P08: its offers got worse after our last move. Propose its best earlier package (it offered it
        itself, so it will most likely agree) instead of pushing further."""
        if not self.cfg.recall_best or getattr(t, "recalled_once", False):
            return []
        seen = [(self.C(t, s2["terms"]), s2["terms"]) for m in t.events if m.get("from") not in ("buyer", "arena")
                for s2 in m.get("term_sheets") or [] if must_haves_ok(self.case, s2["terms"], t.std)]
        if len(seen) < 2 or not t.sheets:
            return []
        now = min(self.C(t, s2["terms"]) for s2 in t.sheets)
        best_c, best_terms = min(seen, key=lambda z: z[0])
        if self.cfg.guards and best_c >= self.c_open * 0.999:
            return []  # its best earlier package is its opening: agreeing to it scores 0
        if best_c < now * 0.997:
            t.recalled_once = True
    def push(self, t, sh):
        """A small ask below its standing price, same terms, before we accept."""
        t.pushes += 1
        ask = complete_offer(self.case, {**sh["terms"], "unit_price": round(sh["terms"]["unit_price"] * (1 - self.cfg.push_pct), 2)})
        self.note("push", supplier=t.sid, n=t.pushes, ask=ask, c=round(self.C(t, ask)))

Sunday's release is in and checked. It sits at `starter-kit/data/release-sunday`, where the engine picks it up automatically, so no `ARENA_RELEASE` setting is needed.

- **Merge:** 11 new data IDs, none clashing with the existing 10,356, and all citable.
- **Tests:** 151 passed with the release in place.

**What's in it:** 6 news items, 4 supplier letters and our company memo. Three things could matter in a hidden case:

- **Prices frozen centrally.** Nordmark (the P02 supplier) and Mairhofer, now part of the Strelvo group, both say "no individual price reductions" for 2027 and offer to talk payment terms and call-off planning. Our engine already detects a frozen price and moves to other terms.
- **Cash-short suppliers.**
  - Fuchsreiter, a P05 supplier, has put its turning department on short-time work. It asks us to pay invoices within 10 days.
  - A credit insurer withdrew cover for Weißacher.
  - Kalwisz (the P11 supplier) filed for insolvency, and the news advises securing supply.
- **Rupprecht-Kessel** (the P16 supplier) bought its bar steel forward at fixed prices until June 2027. Falling steel prices we cite won't move it before then. That costs nothing but a wasted fact.

**The one real exposure:** the engine judges a supplier's need for cash from the frozen credit data. For Fuchsreiter that gives a 10 % cost of money, while the letter says it badly needs cash now. The research session's simulator showed cash-short suppliers as our only remaining weak spot. Our P05 asks already include a 14-day payment package, so that case is covered. A hidden one-supplier case with Fuchsreiter could still go worse.

I'd rather not change the engine on a letter four hours before the freeze without a test. The research session is reading the same release, and its simulator could test the fix. I can't ask it right now: my messages are paused until you write here again.

**Next for me:** the 09:00 pre-flight session on practice.

# makeAnother.md · a buyer agent for the Tacto Negotiation Arena

EHL Grand Finale 2026, Tacto track. Our agent negotiates by e-mail with Tacto's supplier bots for Hollerau
Pumpenwerke: price increases, renewals, RFQs with several bidders, bundles, raw-material surcharges, capacity
cuts and quality cases. It closes the deal with the lowest total cost C, or walks away when the alternative is
cheaper. Forked from [tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit](https://github.com/tacto-ai/negotiation-arena-kit).

Practice board on the evening before the final: mean best score **0.736** over the 10 hosted suppliers, #3 of 24;
a full fresh pass of the final build scores **0.72-0.73** with 10 deals out of 10 and no failed accept.

## How it negotiates

The code decides every number; a language model only writes the words around them.

1. **A target cost.** For every allowed combination of the case's levers (payment days, contract months, lead
   time, Incoterm, index clause, quality terms) the engine solves the unit price at which the supplier's cash
   value equals its estimated cost floor - from our should-cost, its own cost breakdown or letter, its cited
   cost drivers - and costs that package with the arena's published formula. The cheapest one is our target
   (`starter-kit/proto/target.py`).
2. **Packages of equal cost to us.** Each e-mail carries two term sheets that cost us the same but differ in what
   the supplier may value: longer contract, faster payment, its standard lead time, its own index clause at the
   deadband cheapest for us. A term the supplier insists on becomes part of every package.
3. **Visible concessions, then patience.** Our goal moves from the target towards the supplier's standing offer
   over four rounds (early concessions beat holding firm on every supplier we met), but we hold our ask while
   the supplier is still giving at least 0.3 % a round - and accept at once when it goes final or agrees.
4. **Evidence the arena can check.** Every claim carries a data ID from the package: a falling cost driver, our
   orders of the same part elsewhere, its scorecard, our forecast, the notice period in its own letter, the
   rival's offer in an RFQ. Facts that rose, or that argue for the supplier, are never cited; in an RFQ a shared
   fact goes to one bidder only, since the arena counts each ID once per case.
5. **RFQs.** One worker per supplier on its own 60-second clock; the cheapest quote is opened first and the
   others are opened citing its fresh reply; the best standing offer is accepted the moment it is agreed or
   final, a rival's reply in flight gets at most 15 seconds.
6. **Answers.** Volume questions get our binding need and forecast, requests about fixed terms get a plain
   "fixed in this enquiry", complaints about late payment get a promise to pay on the agreed day.
7. **The e-mail.** Claude Sonnet 5.5 rewrites the engine's template; every sentence with a data ID stays
   verbatim, no figure the code did not choose gets in, and the template goes out whenever the model is slow or
   breaks a rule. On the practice suppliers wording did not move the score; the numbers did.

The engine is Tugra's deterministic engine (`starter-kit/proto/`, algorithm `A9h`), developed by the team on
the hosted sandbox, 70 practice sessions and the local simulator. Our earlier agent, the orchestra
(`arena_kit/agents/orchestra.py`), is the fallback if the engine cannot start on a case.

## Setup

Python 3.12 and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). Secrets go into `.env` at the repo root (never committed):

| Variable | What |
|---|---|
| `ARENA_API_KEY` | the team's arena key |
| `CLAUDE_API_KEY` | Anthropic key for the e-mail writer (aliased to `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) |

`starter-kit/.env` holds the non-secret settings: `ARENA_URL`, `ARENA_DATA=data/package`, `LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic`,
`LLM_MODEL=claude-sonnet-5-5`, `LLM_EFFORT=low`.

```bash
cd starter-kit
uv sync --all-extras
uv run arena data                                  # the data package (and Sunday's release, once public)
uv run pytest -q                                   # 70 tests
uv run arena run --set sandbox --agent hybrid      # free: the two demo cases
```

## The Live Final

```bash
cd starter-kit
uv run arena run --set final --agent hybrid --parallel 10 -v > ../logs/final.log 2>&1
```

Started before 12:00 and left running: it waits for each wave, plays its cases in parallel, closes every case
before the wave's cap, retries a case refused for the key's session limit, resumes a running session after a
restart, and never reads `/v1/events`, `/screen`, `/leaderboard` or `/results`. `uv run arena dashboard` shows
every negotiation live at http://127.0.0.1:8765 from our own event log.

## Layout

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `starter-kit/proto/` | the engine: `engine.py` (tactics as `Config` fields, the negotiation loops), `target.py` (target cost), `practice.py` (facts and floors from the data package), `variants.py` (named algorithms) |
| `starter-kit/arena_kit/agents/hybrid.py` | runs the engine through the kit's runner: event log, resume, wave cap, background attachments |
| `starter-kit/arena_kit/agents/engine_writer.py` | the LLM writer and its guards |
| `starter-kit/arena_kit/` | the kit: client, runner (`play.py`), cost function (`cost.py`), data package, dashboard, local simulator |
| `starter-kit/tests/` | 70 tests: cost model, clock rules, RFQ accept timing, the writer's guards, the final runner |
| `vault/` | the team's Obsidian vault: decisions (`Team-Knowledge/Decisions/`), test log (`Progress/Testing.md`), every practice run with its replay |
| `brief/`, `data/` | Tacto's brief, API docs and data package |

## What we learned (short)

- A supplier's first counter barely depends on our first ask; it moves when we move, and when a fact it can
  verify arrives - once per fact.
- Equal-cost packages let the supplier pick the lever it values; the clause at the widest deadband, the longest
  contract and its standard lead time are nearly free for us and worth real money to it.
- Accepting too early cost more than asking too little: three patient rounds while the supplier still gives
  were worth +0.03 on the mean.
- The 60-second clock runs from the supplier's reply; downloading its attachments before reading the offer, or
  waiting for a rival, lost deals until both happened in the background.
- Wording, tone and even the choice of writer model did not change scores on these suppliers; data and timing did.

Decisions, measurements and the Sunday checklist: `vault/Team-Knowledge/Decisions/0007 The final build.md`.

Probably not. A heavily overfitted single pass would land around **0.80**, and reaching 0.85 would mean beating the best result anyone has shown on most of the 10 cases.

**Ceiling if every case matched the best result we know of**

| Case | Our single pass now | Best known | Gain to the mean |
|---|---|---|---|
| P05 | 0.85-0.88 | 0.965 (record) | +0.009 |
| P18 | ~0.50 | 0.727 (record) | +0.023 |
| P08 | ~0.61 | 0.752 (Tacto's house agent) | +0.014 |
| P07 | ~0.70 | 0.782 (Tacto's house agent) | +0.008 |
| P01, P02, P03, P04, P10, P11 | 0.93, 0.735, 0.92, 0.81-0.86, 0.67, 0.71 | no better result known to us | 0 |

Matching every known best takes us from 0.743 to about **0.80**. The remaining 0.05 would have to come from P10, P11, P04 and P02, each gaining about +0.13. Nobody has shown how:
- **P02:** our offline replay tops out at 0.761.
- **P10, P11:** they stop well above the theoretical best price (P10 by about 15 %), and no session of ours ever got below that plateau.

**Two facts about the board:**
- The top teams' ~0.79 is the average of their **best result per case over 300-413 sessions**, not one pass. Even best-of-hundreds hasn't reached 0.85.
- Our 0.743 is a single fresh pass. Our own best-of-n would already be higher.

**What overengineering could still buy:** the bots are nearly deterministic. The same history of term sheets gave identical prices 77-83 % of the time. So with no concern for overfitting, the strongest approach would be a per-case search:
1. Spend 30-50 practice sessions per case exploring different ask sequences, especially in the rounds before each supplier's final offer.
2. Hard-code the best path found for each case and replay it.

That could reach the records on P05 and P18 and maybe the house agent's level on P07 and P08. That's the 0.80 path. It needs roughly 300-500 sessions and a lot of time, and is worth nothing on the final's hidden suppliers.

**Why the last gap is so hard:** the research session's night work closed the ideas we could see in our data:
- More facts don't move a supplier's final price.
- A second fact in the same e-mail adds nothing.
- Slower or faster pacing both did worse.
- Approval steps only exist for two suppliers.

Our paths on P08 and P18 are near-deterministic (5.5 → 5.5 → 5.4 final), so our data never explored what the record holders did. The remaining gap is unexplored supplier behaviour, not modelling we got wrong.

We can't see how they negotiate. Only the public board is visible, not their sessions. But the board says quite a lot.

**The 0.88 is a best-of-many score, not one pass.** The board's `best_mean` averages each team's best score per case over everything they ran. NoIdea ran 484 practice sessions today and holds 8 of the 10 case records. We ran the most of any team (625), and our best-of-many is 0.767 (rank 11). Our single fresh pass is 0.743. So it isn't just volume: they get further on specific cases.

| Case | Record (holder) | Tacto's house agent | Our best |
|---|---|---|---|
| P01 | **1.000** (NoIdea) | 0.966 | ~0.95 |
| P02 | 0.888 (NoIdea) | 0.740 | ~0.76 |
| P03 | 0.989 (NoIdea) | 0.925 | ~0.92 |
| P04 | 0.874 (**us**) | 0.860 | 0.874 |
| P05 | 0.965 (NoIdea) | 0.555 | 0.878 |
| P07 | 0.825 (NoIdea) | 0.782 | ~0.71 |
| P08 | 0.916 (NoIdea) | 0.752 | ~0.66 |
| P10 | 0.741 (NoIdea) | 0.686 | ~0.68 |
| P11 | 0.885 (NoIdea) | 0.314 | ~0.71 |
| P18 | 0.756 (Codacabana) | 0.386 | ~0.53 |

The gaps are structural on P02, P08 and P11 (0.13-0.26), not noise.

**What the evidence points to.** This is inference, not knowledge:
1. **They ask for the theoretical best deal and wait for a yes.** P01 at exactly 1.000 means they closed exactly the cheapest package any supplier would accept. That deal can be computed offline to the cent, as the research session showed overnight. Our engine instead starts below its estimate of the supplier's floor, concedes toward the supplier's offer round by round, and takes the final offer. So the "plateau" we kept hitting is at least partly made by our own concessions. Suppliers can go lower, and theirs did.
2. **They negotiate much longer.** The board's "longest" stat is NoIdea on P05: 33 rounds. Our P05 sessions take 7-10 replies; we accept once a supplier goes final or meets our goal.
3. **They harvest rare "accept" decisions.** The research session's model shows an AI decision layer (counter, hold, final, accept) on top of the price rules. A firm ask at the floor, repeated many times, can occasionally draw an "accept". Over 484 sessions the best one becomes the record.

**What it means for the final:** each case gets one attempt, so best-of-many doesn't carry over. NoIdea's single-pass average is unknown and could be far below 0.88. Point 1 is the lesson that would transfer: aim exactly at the cheapest-acceptable package and stop conceding toward the supplier's plateau. But that's a big change to the negotiation strategy. With development closed at 11:00 and the freeze at 12:00, it can't be tested properly in time. Last night's probes also showed both ways it could go wrong: asking far beyond the supplier's room hardened P08/P18, and slower pacing pushed suppliers to an earlier, higher final offer.

def goal(self, rnd):
        best = self.best_standing()
        ref = self.c_open if self.cfg.toward == "open" else (best[0] if best else self.c_open)
        ref = min(ref, self.c_alt)
        start = self.target_c * (1 + self.cfg.anchor)
        if self.cfg.bottleneck_anchor and self.b.get("category_goal") == "secure_supply":
            # practice P10: never far below a bottleneck's opening PRICE (its opening C is inflated when it covers
            # only part of the need), but always with full coverage: the cheapest such package at that price
            start = max(start, self.bottleneck_floor_c())
        prior = ROOM_PRIOR.get(self.b.get("category_goal"))
        if self.cfg.target_prior and prior and self.c_open < float("inf"):
            # practice P07: our data floor gave a first ask above the best possible deal; never be more timid

            start = min(start, self.c_open * (1 - prior))
        if self.cfg.ask_cap and self.c_open < float("inf"):
